summary: The ed.py command layer closely follows GNU ed 1.19 and every errata item traced correctly. The custom regex parser in posixre.py has two concrete syntax divergences on in-scope expressions. In BRE, a quantifier after a leading ^ binds to the anchor instead of starting a new expression. In ERE, an unmatched ')' is rejected even though POSIX and glibc treat it as a literal.

missing_dependencies: task.toml is not in the packet manifest or directory listing
tests/Dockerfile is not in the packet, as expected for this axis (no tests surface)

findings.claim: In BRE, repetition operators after a leading '^' are applied to the anchor or to an anchor-plus-literal-star composite. GNU ed (glibc regcomp) instead starts a new expression after the anchor. As a result, ^**, ^*\+, ^*\{n\}, ^\+ and ^\? match different text from GNU ed 1.19.

finding_evidence.expected_behavior: In the manual, '*' at the start of an RE matches itself (ed.txt:517-521), and so do '\+' and '\?' at the start of an RE or subexpression (ed.txt:555-566). POSIX BRE makes '*' literal after an initial '^'. glibc parse_expression returns right after an ANCHOR token, so the next operator is parsed at expression start. The reference already follows this rule for a single '*' (posixre.py:169-171) and for '\{' (posixre.py:100, consistent with errata 4). So ^** means '^' followed by zero or more '*', and ^\+ means '^' followed by a literal '+'.
finding_evidence.actual_behavior: posixre.py:166-171 consumes '^*' as one atom, ('cat', [bol, '*']). concat (line 73) then passes that atom to quantifiers(). There the anchor test (line 78) is false for a 'cat' node, and the BRE '*' check (line 85) only tests 'repeated'. A following '*', '\+', '\?' or '\{n\}' therefore repeats the whole (^\*) group. For a bare '^' followed by '\+' or '\?', the BRE branch at lines 94-98 has no anchor check, so it builds rep(bol).
finding_evidence.trace_or_receipt: Static trace, not executed. (1) Line '**x', command s/^**/X/: the atom is cat(bol,'*') and the second '*' makes rep(cat,0,inf). Iteration 1 matches bol at 0 and '*' up to 1. Iteration 2 needs bol at 1, which fails (line 365). The match is [0,1), giving 'X*x'. GNU gives ^ plus \** matching [0,2), so 'Xx'. (2) Line '+a', command s/^\+/X/: this compiles to rep(bol,1,inf), which matches the empty string at 0, giving 'X+a'. GNU gives 'Xa'. (3) Line 'abc', command s/^\+/X/: GNU finds no match, prints '?', and exits non-zero when stdin is a regular file. The reference prints nothing extra and writes 'Xabc'. (4) Line '**', command s/^*\{2\}/X/: this compiles to two copies of (bol,'*'). The second bol fails, so the reference reports No match and '?'. GNU matches '**'.

findings.reachable_case_or_path: Buffer line '**x', script: 's/^**/X/', then ',p', then 'q'. Pipe that to python3 /app/pyed/ed.py -s FILE. The reference prints '*' from the unmatched second star ('X*x'), while GNU ed 1.19 prints 'Xx'. A similar case is s/^\+/X/ on line 'abc', where GNU prints '?' and the reference substitutes.
findings.graded_effect: Standard output, file contents and the exit status (on the no-match variant) all differ from GNU ed 1.19. The instruction compares all three byte for byte. Any hidden script that uses these in-contract BRE forms would fail the reference, or else its goldens would be regenerated from GNU and disagree with the reference.
findings.root_invariant: In BRE, the position right after a start anchor (at the start of the RE, after \( or after \|) is an expression start. '*', '\+' and '\?' there are literal characters that can themselves be quantified. '\{' there is an error.
sibling_variants: ^** (second star repeats the anchor composite instead of the literal star)
the same forms after \( or \|, where concat starts again with start=True (posixre.py:65-75, 190-198), e.g. \(^**\) and a\|^\+
interaction_variants: Global commands: g/^\+/d with -s selects every line in the reference, but only lines starting with '+' in GNU ed.
s with the g suffix: s/^\+/X/g on a line without '+' fails in GNU and succeeds in the reference.
Address search: /^\?/ matches the first following line in the reference, but only a line starting with '?' in GNU ed.
findings.minimal_repair_boundary: Make the BRE parser treat the token after any start anchor as a new expression start. Return the bare ('bol',) atom and let concat parse the next item with start=True, so '*' and the escaped '+' and '?' become literal atoms that later quantifiers can apply to. Stop bundling '^*' into a composite atom.
closure_evidence: s/^\+/X/ on '+a' yields 'Xa' and on 'abc' fails with '?'
the existing ^* and ^\{2\} (error) behaviour is unchanged

findings.claim: With -E, an unmatched ')' makes the reference reject the regular expression. POSIX ERE and glibc (RE_SYNTAX_POSIX_EXTENDED includes RE_UNMATCHED_RIGHT_PAREN_ORD) treat an unmatched ')' as an ordinary character, so GNU ed 1.19 -E accepts it.

finding_evidence.expected_behavior: The instruction puts extended regular expressions in scope and requires GNU ed 1.19 behaviour (instruction.md:1, 7). The manual says only that -E uses extended regular expressions (ed.txt:275-278), so ERE syntax follows POSIX and glibc regcomp(REG_EXTENDED). POSIX makes ')' special only when it matches a preceding '(', and glibc parses an unmatched ')' as a CHARACTER token. So with -E, /a)/ matches the text 'a)'.
finding_evidence.actual_behavior: Parser.concat (posixre.py:68) stops at any ')' in ERE mode because at_close() is true at line 55, even at nesting depth 0. alt() returns, and parse() (lines 42-46) finds i != len(s) and raises RegexError. Ed.compile_regex (ed.py:430-437) turns that into 'Invalid regular expression', and the command fails with '?'.
finding_evidence.trace_or_receipt: Static trace, not executed. With -E, line 'a)b', command s/a)/X/: get_pattern_for_s returns 'a)', and set_subst_regex calls compile_regex, which calls Regex('a)', ere=True). parse, then alt, then concat reads atom 'a'. at_close() is true, so concat returns. alt sees no '|' and returns, and parse raises because i=1 != 2. command_s returns False, the main loop prints '?', and with a regular-file stdin the process exits with status 1. GNU ed -E compiles 'a)' with ')' as a literal and substitutes, giving 'Xb'.

findings.reachable_case_or_path: Run python3 /app/pyed/ed.py -E -s FILE, where FILE holds the line 'f(x) = y)'. Script: 's/y)/z/', then ',p', then 'q'. GNU ed 1.19 prints 'f(x) = z'. The reference prints '?' and stops with a regular-file stdin, or with a pipe prints '?' and then the unchanged line.
findings.graded_effect: Standard output, the resulting file contents and the exit status differ from GNU ed 1.19 for any -E script that uses an unmatched ')'. This form is in-contract POSIX ERE syntax.
findings.root_invariant: In ERE, ')' is a group closer only when it matches an open '('. At nesting depth 0 it is an ordinary character.
sibling_variants: a lone ')' as the whole ERE (concat returns empty and parse raises)
(a))b, where the second ')' is at depth 0
a|), where ')' starts the second branch at depth 0
the BRE counterpart \) is correctly rejected when unmatched (glibc POSIX_BASIC lacks the flag), so it is not affected
interaction_variants: Address search: -E with /x)/ fails in the reference but finds the line in GNU ed.
Global command: -E with g/)/d errors before any line is deleted in the reference.
Regular-file stdin: the spurious error ends the script early, so later commands and writes never run.
findings.minimal_repair_boundary: Track the group nesting depth in the ERE parser. At depth 0, do not let at_close() end concat; parse ')' as a literal atom there.

Checked the leftmost-longest search and memoisation in Regex._walk/search: longest end retained, capture priority is first DFS path, repc run memo.

Checked BRE and ERE syntax cases against POSIX/glibc: consecutive duplication, anchors in context, \| in BRE and ERE, brackets with classes and ranges, back-reference closure. This found CRS-1 and CRS-2.
Considered [a-m-o]-style ranges (glibc REG_ERANGE; the reference accepts them). Excluded because POSIX leaves them undefined and the manual does not describe them.

unresolved_checks.concern: After a regular expression fails to compile, GNU ed 1.19 may forget the previous pattern (its compile slot is regfree'd before regcomp), so a following // would fail with 'No previous pattern'. The reference keeps last_regexp unchanged on failure (ed.py:430-437).
unresolved_checks.missing_evidence: Either the GNU ed 1.19 regex.c source or a GNU ed receipt for the script '/fo/', then '/\(/', then '//' on a buffer containing 'foo'.

unresolved_checks.concern: For nested repetitions, the capture groups chosen by the reference's priority-ordered DFS with (instruction, position) memoisation may differ from glibc's sifted-state set_regs choice. That would change \N replacement text without changing the overall match.
unresolved_checks.missing_evidence: GNU ed receipts for nested-repeat capture cases such as s/\(\(a*\)b\)*/[\1|\2]/ on varied inputs.
